transcript.content: Hello, welcome in—I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. Smith. Thank you for fitting me in. Um, well, what brings me in... it's a bit of a long story, I guess, but I'll try to give you the context because I think it matters. I'm 46, I work as a software developer, and I've always had a lot of plates spinning at once. I kind of thought that was just how my brain operated best, you know? Just always having a dozen projects going. But lately, things have just gotten completely out of hand and I feel like I'm drowning in my own life. 

What finally pushed me to come in and actually make this appointment is that I just can’t seem to organize the moving parts anymore. And there are so, so many moving parts right now. I’ve got these complex patent notes I need to finalize for a new architecture we're building at work, and at the exact same time, I’m supposed to be doing all this workshop prep for the junior developers. Then, outside of my main job, I have these gallery deadlines coming up for some interactive digital art installations I do, which is a whole other stressor, plus just the day-to-day team decisions I have to manage... it's just a mountain of information. 

And the problem is, instead of looking at it all and making a logical plan, I just can't sort it out. I sit down at my desk and I end up starting whatever is loudest instead of what actually matters. Like, whatever email just chimed or whoever is pinging me on Slack gets my immediate attention, while the major, critical deadlines just completely fall by the wayside. I'll spend three hours on some minor formatting issue just because it was right in front of my face. I just... I can't seem to prioritize or get a grip on the structure of it all anymore, and it's really starting to catch up with me.

Would you say this kind of difficulty organizing tasks and getting distracted has been a pattern for you since childhood or early adulthood, or is this really a new change that started somewhat recently?

Well, that's the thing, isn't it? It's funny you ask that, because for the longest time, I just thought this was how adulthood was supposed to feel—just this constant, overwhelming rush of things to do. But when I really sit down and think about it... when I really look back, I realize it’s not new at all. It’s always been there, just... maybe the stakes were lower back then? 

Like, if I go all the way back to grade school—and I'm talking early elementary school, second or third grade—my parents saved all my old report cards, and it's almost comical reading them now. Every single teacher, year after year, wrote almost the exact same thing. They’d say, "He's very bright, he grasps the concepts," but then there was always the "but." "But he spends half the day daydreaming," or "He stares out the window during math." And the homework... oh, the homework. I would actually do the work, sit there at the kitchen table and finish the worksheet, but then I'd just... forget to turn it in. Or I'd lose the entire homework folder on the bus ride to school. 

I remember this one specific time in fourth grade, I had to do a diorama on the solar system, and I spent hours painting these little styrofoam planets. I was so proud of it. But when the day came to present it, I had left it sitting right on the dining room table. I just walked out the door without it. So, yeah, this inability to keep track of things, this getting lost in my own head... it was definitely there long before I was even a teenager. It just feels like now, instead of a styrofoam planet, I'm forgetting critical patent filings, you know? The pattern is exactly the same, it's just the consequences that have grown up.

When you find yourself jumping to the loudest task instead of the important one, is that happening because you're preoccupied with anxious, worried thoughts about things going wrong, or does it happen even when you're not feeling particularly worried?

No, it's... you know, it's really not worry. I wouldn't call it anxiety at all, actually. It's almost the opposite sometimes? Like, if I were actively panicking about the patent notes, maybe the adrenaline would actually force me to look at them. But this happens even when I'm having a perfectly fine, calm day. Like, I could have had a great morning, drank my coffee, sat down at my desk feeling completely fine, no dread whatsoever... and it still happens exactly the same way. 

Just to give you an example of how it goes, just last Tuesday I sat down to work on those architecture notes. I wasn't stressed. But then a Slack notification popped up from one of the junior devs. And it wasn't a crisis, he just had a question about a hex code for a button on a staging server. Something incredibly minor that he probably could have found himself. But because it literally slid across my screen and made a noise at that exact second, my brain just entirely shifted gears. I didn't just reply with the color code. I opened up the design files, started looking at the whole color palette, realized the contrast ratio wasn't totally optimized for accessibility standards, and... well, before I knew it, I had spent two and a half hours rewriting the CSS variables for our entire component library. 

I wasn't avoiding the patent notes because I was worried about them or afraid of messing them up. I just... I honestly just forgot they existed for those two hours. It's like my brain has no working memory for priorities. Whatever is newest, whatever is flashing or pinging right in front of my face, it just completely overwrites my mental RAM, if that makes sense. I'm not sitting there chewing my nails or obsessing over worst-case scenarios, I'm just completely, totally absorbed in the distraction. The anxiety only really hits after the fact, you know? When it's 4 PM and I realize I've done absolutely nothing on the one critical thing I needed to do. 

So people always assume I'm procrastinating out of fear or stress, but in the moment, I'm actually not feeling worried at all, just... hijacked, I guess. It's really frustrating trying to explain that to my project managers, because they always ask what they can do to lower my stress to help me focus, and I have to tell them it's not the stress, it's just the... well, it's just the way my attention gets pulled. Because even if they take away the stressful

Aside from the distractibility, do you notice things like feeling physically restless, needing to move or fidget, interrupting others, or acting impulsively—blurting things out or making snap decisions—that have also been present since childhood?

Well, the blurting things out or making snap decisions... no, I don't really do that. I'm actually pretty quiet in meetings, probably because I'm usually lost in my own thoughts anyway. But the physical restlessness? Oh, absolutely. That is... yeah, that's a big one. 

It's actually becoming a bit of a tricky issue with remote work right now. We have these incredibly long design calls—sometimes they go on for two, maybe three hours when we're mapping out all the dependencies for the new architecture—and sitting still for that long is just... I can't do it. I literally feel this pressure building up in my body, like this physical need to move that just gets tighter and tighter the longer I sit there. It’s like my muscles just have to fire or I’m going to crawl out of my skin. 

So I end up pacing around my office. I have to turn my camera off sometimes, or I try to frame the webcam just right so I can stand up, and I'll just pace back and forth behind my desk. Or I'll shift from my main ergonomic chair to this little armchair I have in the corner, just constantly moving from chair to chair, even when I’m really trying to look focused and professional for the project managers. I just can't stay anchored to one spot. I've probably worn a literal track into the rug at this point just from walking back and forth while people are talking. 

And, you know, since you asked about childhood, it was the exact same way back then. I remember my mom always reaching over and putting her hand on my knee at the dinner table because I was constantly bouncing my leg and shaking the whole table. She used to call it the 'earthquake.' I didn't even realize I was doing it half the time, it was just this automatic release valve for that pressure. So yeah, I don't really

Have you ever had distinct periods—lasting several days or more—where you felt unusually elated, needed much less sleep than normal, or felt like your thoughts were racing much more than usual, separate from your everyday pattern of distractibility and restlessness?

No, no, nothing like that. I mean, I've never had a time where I felt... what did you say, unusually elated? No. My thoughts are always a bit noisy, sure, like I was saying about the Slack messages and getting pulled into the CSS variables, but it's not like a racing, euphoric kind of thing. It's more just... scattered. Like a radio scanning stations, not a high-speed train, if that makes sense.

And as for the sleep thing, needing less sleep? Oh, I definitely need my sleep. If I don't get my solid seven or eight hours, I am an absolute wreck the next day. The brain fog just gets ten times worse. I mean, sure, there are nights where I might stay up way too late because I've gone down some ridiculous rabbit hole on Wikipedia about, I don't know, the history of the Byzantine Empire or something, or I'm trying to fix a stubborn bug in my code and I just completely lose track of time. 

I remember this one time a few months ago, I was trying to migrate this legacy database, and I ended up staying awake until like 4 AM. But I wasn't elated, and I certainly didn't *need* less sleep—I was exhausted. My eyes were burning, I was practically falling out of my chair, but I just couldn't pull myself away from the screen until the script finally finished running without throwing an error. And the next day, I was completely useless. I had to drink about four cups of coffee just to make it through our morning standup meeting, and even then I felt like a zombie. 

So, no, I don't get those days-long stretches of feeling energized or euphoric or feeling like I don't need to rest. It's really just the everyday, baseline struggle of trying to keep my attention pointed in the right direction. It never really escalates into anything like what you're describing with the racing thoughts and the elation. It's just this constant, steady hum of distraction, you know? I'm actually pretty even-keeled mood-wise, just... chronically disorganized, and usually pretty tired from trying to compensate for it all day.

Childhood-onset inattention and hyperactivity/restlessness confirmed, without impulsivity blurting or mania. Distractibility not anxiety-driven, consistent with ADHD combined presentation persisting into adulthood.
